THE FINANCIAL BLINDSPOT  
One of the biggest mistakes investors make is assuming that whatever worked over the last few years will keep working forever. I made that mistake with real estate, and I think a lot of investors are making a similar mistake today with stocks. The investments making you the most money can also quietly create the most risk.

THE CONCENTRATION TRAP  
A lot of people think owning an S&P 500 index fund automatically means they are fully diversified. But roughly 10 companies now make up more than a third of the entire index. That means a surprisingly large percentage of your money could be tied to the same handful of businesses.

WHY CONCENTRATION CAN BECOME DANGEROUS  
Concentration feels great when the biggest companies keep winning. The problem is that if those companies struggle, the rest of the index may not be able to offset the decline. That is similar to what happened to me with real estate, where I owned multiple properties but they were all exposed to the same city and the same risks.

AI CAN WIN AND INVESTORS CAN STILL LOSE  
I believe artificial intelligence will change almost everything, but that does not mean every AI investment works out. During the dot-com bubble, the internet absolutely changed the world, but companies like Cisco still lost enormous amounts of value. You can be right about the technology and still pay the wrong price.

THE RISK RESET  
My goals today are different from when I first started investing. Years ago, I was focused almost entirely on maximizing growth. Today, I care much more about stability, flexibility, and protecting what I have already built.

MY 2027 INVESTING PLAN  
Most of my portfolio is still invested in low cost U.S. and international index funds. I also have roughly 15% to 20% in tax-free municipal bonds, around 10% to 12% in a Bitcoin ETF, and the rest spread between cash and personal-use real estate. What is changing is where I am putting new money.

MORE INTERNATIONAL EXPOSURE  
I still like the S&P 500, but I am not completely comfortable having so much exposure dependent on the same handful of companies. Because of that, I am gradually increasing my international allocation.

MORE BONDS  
I am also putting more money into tax-free municipal bonds. At this stage, I like having part of my portfolio generating relatively predictable income without the same level of volatility as stocks.

MORE CASH AND FLEXIBILITY  
I am being more intentional about keeping cash available. If we experience a prolonged downturn, I want to be able to ride it out without changing my lifestyle or being forced to sell.

REBALANCING BITCOIN WITHOUT SELLING  
I am still invested in Bitcoin, but it has become a larger percentage of my portfolio than I would ideally want. Rather than selling it, I plan to balance the allocation by directing new money elsewhere.

THE STRESS TEST  
Before 2027, look at everything you own and ask how much of your money is really riding on the same bet. Then decide what you would do if markets fell 20%, 30%, or 40%.

YOU DO NOT HAVE TO SELL EVERYTHING  
If your portfolio is more concentrated than you want, you can simply redirect new contributions toward areas where you want more exposure.

THE BIGGEST LESSON  
There is no single strategy that makes sense for every stage of life. When you are younger, time, savings rate, and consistently investing may matter most. As wealth grows, preservation and flexibility can become more important. The goal is not to maximize every possible dollar. It is to build a portfolio that gives you freedom without becoming something you constantly worry about.

ONE OF THE BIGGEST WEALTH BUILDING OPPORTUNITIES?  
Despite inflation, high interest rates, geopolitical uncertainty, and concerns around AI spending, several factors are lining up that could create a major economic and investing opportunity over the next few years.

THE BIGGEST RISKS RIGHT NOW  
Oil remains one of the biggest wildcards. Higher energy prices feed directly into inflation, which keeps pressure on the Federal Reserve to maintain higher interest rates. At the same time, the United States continues running enormous deficits, while companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars building AI infrastructure.

VALUATIONS ARE STILL HIGH  
The Shiller CAPE ratio remains near historically elevated levels, which suggests investors are paying a premium for future growth. However, high valuations alone do not necessarily mean stocks are about to crash, especially if corporate earnings continue growing quickly.

THE 80 YEAR MIDTERM STREAK  
Historically, the S&P 500 has been higher one year after every midterm election since 1946, with an average gain of roughly 14%. That does not guarantee future returns, but removing election uncertainty has historically been positive for markets.

MARKET DROPS ARE NORMAL  
Even during long term bull markets, corrections happen regularly. The S&P 500 has historically experienced a 10% decline about once every 18 months and a 20% decline roughly once every six years. Those drops can feel catastrophic in the moment, but they have also historically created some of the strongest future returns.

STOCKS MAY BE CHEAPER THAN THEY LOOK  
While long term valuation measures remain expensive, the S&P 500 is trading at a much lower multiple based on expected future earnings. Corporate profit expectations have grown quickly enough that valuations have actually declined relative to earnings, even with stock prices near record levels.

THE BULL CASE  
Several things could push markets higher. A resolution with Iran could lower oil prices, which could reduce inflation and eventually allow interest rates to come down. Lower rates could support spending, investment, housing, and corporate valuations.

CORPORATE PROFITS ARE SURGING  
S&P 500 companies have reported extremely strong earnings growth, and analysts expect that momentum to continue. If profits keep rising faster than stock prices, valuations could become more reasonable without requiring a major market decline.

AI COULD EXPAND BEYOND BIG TECH  
The biggest AI opportunity may not belong exclusively to companies building chips and data centers. Businesses across the economy could use AI to reduce administrative work, improve productivity, write software faster, lower expenses, and ultimately increase profits.

THE CONSUMER IS STILL HOLDING UP  
Recent job growth came in much stronger than expected while unemployment declined. If inflation falls while wages continue rising, consumers could regain purchasing power, leading to more spending, stronger corporate earnings, and continued economic growth.

DO NOT TRY TO TIME THE SELLOFF  
Some of the market's best days happen extremely close to its worst days. Missing only a handful of those strong rebound days can dramatically reduce long term investment returns, which is why panic selling can be so damaging.

WHAT I’M DOING  
I am cautiously optimistic, but I am not assuming stocks move straight higher. I am continuing to invest consistently, staying diversified, keeping enough liquidity to buy during market declines, and paying close attention to AI productivity. The biggest opportunity may not be predicting the next market move, but having enough financial flexibility to keep investing when everyone else is afraid.

snippet.description:

NOW MIGHT ACTUALLY BE A GOOD TIME TO BUY  
Mortgage rates are around 7.5%, affordability is near record lows, and most people think buying a house right now is a terrible idea. But beneath the surface, the housing market is shifting in a way we have not seen in more than a decade. Sellers now dramatically outnumber buyers, pending sales have fallen, and buyers are finally gaining leverage.

THE AFFORDABILITY TRAP  
The median home sold for roughly $417,500 in September, while mortgage rates have moved sharply higher. On the same house, a higher interest rate can add hundreds of dollars per month to the payment. Buying a home has rarely been this expensive on a monthly basis, which explains why so many buyers have stepped away.

THE HOUSING MARKET IS SPLITTING  
There is no single housing market. Some cities have fallen significantly from their pandemic highs, while others continue reaching new records. Austin, parts of Florida, Seattle, San Jose, and Orlando have seen weakness, while several markets in the Northeast and Midwest remain much stronger.

WHY SOME MARKETS ARE FALLING  
Many of the weakest markets built enormous amounts of new housing during the boom. Prices also rose much faster than local incomes could support, while insurance, taxes, and other ownership costs increased dramatically. When demand slowed, those markets were left with too much inventory and not enough buyers.

WHY OTHER MARKETS KEEP RISING  
Many Northeast and Midwest markets have the opposite problem. There are still relatively few homes for sale, limited new construction, and prices that started from more affordable levels. That supply shortage has helped keep prices elevated even while mortgage rates remain high.

SELLERS NOW OUTNUMBER BUYERS  
Redfin found there are roughly 62.6% more sellers than buyers, the largest gap in its records going back to 2013. Around 41 of the 50 largest U.S. metros are now considered buyer's markets, giving qualified buyers significantly more negotiating power than they had just a few years ago.

SELLERS ARE CUTTING PRICES  
A record share of homes for sale have received price cuts, homes are taking longer to sell, and pending sales remain near historic lows. In some markets, people who bought near the peak are now listing their homes for less than they originally paid.

WHY LOWBALL OFFERS CAN WORK  
Almost no competition, rising inventory, expensive mortgages, and the slower holiday season can create motivated sellers. Instead of paying asking price, buyers may be able to negotiate a lower purchase price, closing costs, repairs, or even a mortgage rate buydown.

THE 2011 COMPARISON  
When I started buying real estate around 2011, almost everyone believed housing was still a terrible investment. Prices had already collapsed, buyers were afraid, and most people wanted to wait until things felt safer. That fear ultimately created some of the best buying opportunities of the entire cycle.

TODAY IS NOT 2011  
Home prices are much higher today, mortgage rates are higher, and there is no guarantee prices have bottomed. I also do not expect the kind of appreciation we saw after 2020. But the sentiment and lack of buyer competition are beginning to look very different from the housing market of just a few years ago.

WHAT I WOULD DO  
If you need to buy a home, this may be one of the better environments in years to negotiate aggressively. Take your time, stay within a payment you can comfortably afford, and submit offers at prices where the numbers actually make sense. You do not need to predict the exact bottom. You just need to find a deal good enough that you are comfortable owning it even if prices fall a little further.

snippet.title: BREAKING: The Fed Just Froze Rates — Here’s What Happens After EVERY Midterm Since 1950!
snippet.description:
Thanks to SoFi for sponsoring the video! Click here to sign-up for SoFi Crypto: https://sofi.com/graham | Let's talk about the Federal Reserve Rate Pause and what this means for the stock market / economy going forward - Enjoy! Add me on Instagram: GPStephan

FOLLOW MY INVESTMENTS / STOCKS HERE: https://getblossom.onelink.me/SOfu/grahamstephan 

START BUILDING WEALTH WITH MY FREE NEWSLETTER: https://grahamstephan.substack.com

INFLATION IS MOVING HIGHER AGAIN  
Inflation climbed back to 3.7% in September, while producer prices rose even faster. Higher oil prices are adding pressure, and that is pushing Treasury yields higher at the exact moment investors were hoping borrowing costs would finally come down.

TREASURY YIELDS ARE SURGING  
Treasury bonds help set borrowing costs throughout the economy, including mortgages, business loans, credit lines, and other debt. When long term yields rise, financing becomes more expensive and investors start comparing risky assets against the return they can earn from government bonds.

WHY HIGHER BOND YIELDS MATTER  
If investors can earn more than 5% from Treasuries, stocks and real estate have to offer a compelling reason to take additional risk. Higher yields can pull money away from more expensive assets and put pressure on valuations across the market.

THE STOCK MARKET IS WEAKER THAN IT LOOKS  
The S&P 500 has performed well this year, but the headline index hides a much weaker market underneath. More than 4 out of 10 S&P 500 stocks are down this year, while a relatively small group of giant technology companies has generated a huge portion of the overall gains.

THE MARKET IS EXTREMELY CONCENTRATED  
Seven of the largest companies now make up more than a third of the S&P 500, while the top 10 represent roughly 40% of the index. That means the performance of a handful of companies can have an enormous impact on an investor who believes they own 500 evenly distributed stocks.

AI IS HOLDING UP THE ECONOMY  
AI spending has become a major driver of economic growth, while other areas are slowing. Job growth has weakened, housing construction is declining, and investors are beginning to question whether hundreds of billions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure will ultimately generate enough profit.

THE AI TRADE IS GETTING TESTED  
Investors have recently punished companies even after strong earnings because of concerns around rising AI spending. If the largest technology companies begin disappointing investors, the concentration of the market means weakness could spread quickly throughout the major indexes.

THE MIDTERM ELECTION EFFECT  
Historically, midterm election years have been more volatile than other years in the presidential cycle. Much of that weakness appears to come from uncertainty over taxes, spending, regulations, and control of Congress.

WHAT HAPPENS AFTER MIDTERMS  
Historically, stocks have often performed strongly once the election is over and uncertainty disappears. Since 1950, the S&P 500 has been higher 12 months after every midterm election, although past performance obviously does not guarantee the same outcome this time.

THE FED PAUSE
The Federal Reserve kept rates unchanged at its latest meeting, but that does not necessarily mean rate hikes are finished. Inflation remains elevated, and the Fed has indicated that future decisions will depend heavily on incoming economic data.

ANOTHER RATE HIKE EXPECTED
Markets are still pricing in the possibility of additional tightening. The best case is that oil prices fall, inflation cools, and the Fed stops raising rates. The worst case is inflation staying elevated while the job market continues weakening.

STOCKS ARE NOT CHEAP  
The CAPE ratio is near levels rarely seen outside the dotcom bubble. At the same time, forward earnings make valuations look less extreme, so the key question is whether corporate profits can grow fast enough to justify current prices.

WHAT I’M DOING  
I am still investing consistently, but I am also keeping some cash, staying diversified, avoiding debt, and maintaining an emergency fund. I am not trying to predict a crash. I just want to be in a position to buy if markets fall instead of being forced to sell.

localized.description:

START BUILDING WEALTH WITH MY FREE NEWSLETTER: https://grahamstephan.substack.com

INFLATION IS MOVING HIGHER AGAIN  
Inflation climbed back to 3.7% in September, while producer prices rose even faster. Higher oil prices are adding pressure, and that is pushing Treasury yields higher at the exact moment investors were hoping borrowing costs would finally come down.

TREASURY YIELDS ARE SURGING  
Treasury bonds help set borrowing costs throughout the economy, including mortgages, business loans, credit lines, and other debt. When long term yields rise, financing becomes more expensive and investors start comparing risky assets against the return they can earn from government bonds.

WHY HIGHER BOND YIELDS MATTER  
If investors can earn more than 5% from Treasuries, stocks and real estate have to offer a compelling reason to take additional risk. Higher yields can pull money away from more expensive assets and put pressure on valuations across the market.

THE STOCK MARKET IS WEAKER THAN IT LOOKS  
The S&P 500 has performed well this year, but the headline index hides a much weaker market underneath. More than 4 out of 10 S&P 500 stocks are down this year, while a relatively small group of giant technology companies has generated a huge portion of the overall gains.

THE MARKET IS EXTREMELY CONCENTRATED  
Seven of the largest companies now make up more than a third of the S&P 500, while the top 10 represent roughly 40% of the index. That means the performance of a handful of companies can have an enormous impact on an investor who believes they own 500 evenly distributed stocks.

AI IS HOLDING UP THE ECONOMY  
AI spending has become a major driver of economic growth, while other areas are slowing. Job growth has weakened, housing construction is declining, and investors are beginning to question whether hundreds of billions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure will ultimately generate enough profit.

THE AI TRADE IS GETTING TESTED  
Investors have recently punished companies even after strong earnings because of concerns around rising AI spending. If the largest technology companies begin disappointing investors, the concentration of the market means weakness could spread quickly throughout the major indexes.

THE MIDTERM ELECTION EFFECT  
Historically, midterm election years have been more volatile than other years in the presidential cycle. Much of that weakness appears to come from uncertainty over taxes, spending, regulations, and control of Congress.

WHAT HAPPENS AFTER MIDTERMS  
Historically, stocks have often performed strongly once the election is over and uncertainty disappears. Since 1950, the S&P 500 has been higher 12 months after every midterm election, although past performance obviously does not guarantee the same outcome this time.

THE FED PAUSE
The Federal Reserve kept rates unchanged at its latest meeting, but that does not necessarily mean rate hikes are finished. Inflation remains elevated, and the Fed has indicated that future decisions will depend heavily on incoming economic data.

ANOTHER RATE HIKE EXPECTED
Markets are still pricing in the possibility of additional tightening. The best case is that oil prices fall, inflation cools, and the Fed stops raising rates. The worst case is inflation staying elevated while the job market continues weakening.

STOCKS ARE NOT CHEAP  
The CAPE ratio is near levels rarely seen outside the dotcom bubble. At the same time, forward earnings make valuations look less extreme, so the key question is whether corporate profits can grow fast enough to justify current prices.

WHAT I’M DOING  
I am still investing consistently, but I am also keeping some cash, staying diversified, avoiding debt, and maintaining an emergency fund. I am not trying to predict a crash. I just want to be in a position to buy if markets fall instead of being forced to sell.

snippet.title: An Urgent Warning For ALL Investors
snippet.description:
Start your 7-day free trial + unlock 4 extra months of Surfshark VPN — head to https://surfshark.com/graham or use code GRAHAM at checkout! | Add me on Instagram: GPStephan

FOLLOW MY INVESTMENTS / STOCKS HERE: https://getblossom.onelink.me/SOfu/grahamstephan 

START BUILDING WEALTH WITH MY FREE NEWSLETTER: https://grahamstephan.substack.com

THE BULL MARKET
The current bull market began in late 2022, and the S&P 500 has returned roughly 129% since then. Every major dip has recovered quickly, reinforcing the belief that buying every decline is easy money. Retail investors are now buying down days at record levels, while the S&P 500 has averaged about 14.8% annually since 2009, far above its long-term average. 

THE LOST DECADE
Markets do not always recover quickly. After the 1929 crash, the Dow took more than 25 years to regain its previous high. From 1966 to 1982, inflation-adjusted returns were disastrous, and from 2000 through 2009, $10,000 invested in the S&P 500 actually fell to roughly $9,089 including dividends. Japan took more than 34 years to regain its 1989 peak.   

VALUATIONS ARE EXTREME
Stocks are more popular than ever, with roughly 33% of American household wealth invested in equities. The Shiller CAPE ratio recently reached about 41, its highest level since 2000, while the 10 largest companies make up around 39% of the S&P 500. Margin debt is also at record levels, increasing the risk if markets reverse.

Several major firms expect weaker returns ahead. Vanguard projects roughly 4% to 5% annual returns for U.S. stocks over the next five to ten years. Goldman previously projected just 3% annually before later increasing its estimate, while GMO has forecast negative real returns for U.S. large-cap stocks. High valuations are the main concern.

Others remain optimistic. Deutsche Bank, Morgan Stanley, and Yardeni have raised S&P 500 targets, supported by strong earnings growth and nearly $8 trillion sitting in money-market funds. Historically, the average post-WWII bull market lasted roughly 5.6 years and gained about 167%, meaning the current bull market is not unusually old yet.

EXPERTS CAN BE VERY WRONG
Major investors predicted further crashes in 2020 and 2022, only for markets to rally dramatically afterward. Some of the strongest opportunities have historically appeared when sentiment was most pessimistic. The lesson is that even highly respected investors cannot reliably predict tops, bottoms, recessions, or future returns.

THE CRASH TEST
A lost decade is much less damaging when you are diversified. From 2000 through 2009, the S&P 500 lost money while bonds nearly doubled and gold performed extremely well. Owning international stocks, bonds, cash, real estate, or other assets can reduce the risk of being completely dependent on one market.  

KEEP INVESTING
Trying to time the market can be extremely costly because many of the best days happen near the worst days. Historically, after the 15 worst 10-year periods for the S&P 500, the following decade was positive every time. Maintaining income, continuing to invest, and avoiding panic selling may matter more than predicting what happens next.  

SURVIVE THE NEXT DECADE
The market could continue rising as earnings grow into today’s valuations, or stocks could spend years moving sideways. The biggest danger is investing so aggressively that a prolonged decline forces you to sell. Diversification, liquidity, manageable risk, and realistic expectations matter because you do not need to predict the next decade. You simply need a portfolio capable of surviving it.

snippet.title: “America’s Debt Spiral Is Going To Implode Within 3 Years” - Ray Dalio’s Final Warning
snippet.description:
Take your personal data back with Incogni! Use code GRAHAM at the link below and get 60% off an annual plan: https://incogni.com/graham | Add me on Instagram: GPStephan

FOLLOW MY INVESTMENTS / STOCKS HERE: https://getblossom.onelink.me/SOfu/grahamstephan 

START BUILDING WEALTH WITH MY FREE NEWSLETTER: https://grahamstephan.substack.com

THE U.S. DEBT SPIRAL  
The United States now owes more than $40 trillion, and the total is still rising by billions of dollars every day. The bigger problem is not just the debt itself, but the growing amount of interest the government has to pay as older, cheaper debt gets refinanced at much higher rates.

WHY INTEREST COSTS MATTER  
For years, the government was able to borrow enormous amounts of money at extremely low rates. Now, with borrowing costs at their highest levels in decades, that strategy is becoming much more expensive. The CBO projects federal interest costs could reach roughly $2.1 trillion per year by 2036.

WHO KEEPS BUYING U.S. DEBT?  
The government funds its deficits by issuing Treasury bonds. That system works as long as investors are willing to keep buying them at reasonable rates. If buyers begin demanding 5%, 6%, or more to lend the government money, interest expenses increase even faster.

FOREIGN BUYERS ARE PULLING BACK  
Countries such as China and Japan have historically been major holders of U.S. Treasuries. Some foreign holdings have recently declined, raising concerns about who will absorb the enormous amount of new debt the United States needs to issue.

THE SUPPLY OF DEBT IS EXPLODING  
At the same time demand is being questioned, Treasury supply continues to rise. The government is running massive deficits, while corporations and AI companies are also borrowing huge amounts of money. All of them are competing for the same pool of capital.

INFLATION MAKES THE PROBLEM WORSE  
Inflation remains above the Federal Reserve’s target, which makes investors less willing to lock money into long term bonds at lower yields. If investors expect inflation or interest rates to remain elevated, they naturally demand a higher return.

THE DOOM LOOP  
Higher yields can create a feedback loop. Higher rates increase government interest costs. Larger interest expenses create bigger deficits. Bigger deficits require more borrowing. More borrowing increases Treasury supply, which can push yields even higher.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR STOCKS  
Higher Treasury yields make stocks less attractive because investors can earn competitive returns without taking as much risk. Growth stocks can be especially vulnerable because more of their value depends on profits expected many years into the future.

MORTGAGE RATES GET HIT TOO  
Mortgage rates generally move with longer term Treasury yields. As those yields rise, homebuyers face larger monthly payments, affordability falls, and the housing market can slow even without the Federal Reserve directly raising mortgage rates.

COMPANIES HAVE TO REFINANCE  
Trillions of dollars of corporate debt comes due over the next several years. Companies that previously borrowed at 3% may have to refinance at rates twice as high, reducing profits and leaving less money for hiring, expansion, dividends, and buybacks.

HOW DOES THIS END?  
The best case is stronger economic growth, potentially helped by AI productivity, allowing the economy to grow faster than the debt. Another possibility is higher inflation and some form of financial repression, where interest rates are kept below inflation to gradually reduce the real value of the debt.

WHAT I’M DOING  
I am not assuming a sudden 2008 style collapse. I am continuing to invest consistently, keeping some money in Treasuries while yields remain attractive, maintaining a cash buffer, and staying diversified across assets. The goal is not to perfectly predict what happens next. It is to be positioned well enough to handle whatever comes.

snippet.description:
Download the FREE Upside App here https://yt.link/8xSk8ez and use code Graham25 to get an extra 25 cents back per gallon on your first tank of gas! Thank you Upside for sponsoring this video! Let's talk about why Americans are running out of money, the dangers to the economy, and what you can do moving forward - Enjoy!

START BUILDING WEALTH WITH MY FREE NEWSLETTER: https://grahamstephan.substack.com

AMERICANS ARE RUNNING OUT OF MONEY
Major CEOs are warning that consumers are stretched thin, with even households earning around $100,000 beginning to shop more cautiously. Mortgage rates are above 7%, gasoline prices have surged, airfare is up sharply, and everyday costs across food, housing, insurance, and transportation continue to climb. 

EVERYDAY COSTS KEEP RISING
New-car payments have hit record highs, used-car prices remain elevated, auto insurance and maintenance cost more, and fuel prices are up significantly. Housing is also more expensive, with higher rents, mortgage payments, utilities, and homeowners insurance. Food and travel costs have increased as well, meaning more of each paycheck is being consumed before discretionary spending even begins. 

WAGES AREN’T KEEPING UP WITH EVERYTHING
Average wages have risen about 4.1%, but many of the largest household expenses are increasing at similar or faster rates. At the same time, borrowing costs for mortgages, credit cards, auto loans, and personal loans have risen, creating a cycle where consumers with less cash available must borrow at increasingly expensive rates.

THE SAVINGS CUSHION IS DISAPPEARING
The personal savings rate has fallen to roughly 3%, meaning the average household is setting aside very little for emergencies. About half of Americans reportedly cannot comfortably cover an unexpected $500 expense, while companies are seeing lower-income households dip into savings simply to maintain normal spending.

THE ECONOMY IS BECOMING K-SHAPED
The top 10% of earners now account for more than half of consumer spending, which can make headline economic data look stronger than the finances of the typical household. Meanwhile, Americans owe roughly $1.26 trillion on credit cards, most cardholders carry balances, and hardship withdrawals from 401(k)s have reached record levels.

THE PRESSURE IS MOVING UP THE INCOME LADDER
Financial stress is no longer limited to the lowest-income households. The Dollar General CEO says even households earning $100,000 or more are beginning to behave like lower-income shoppers. Consumers are first burning through extra cash, then savings, then credit cards, and eventually retirement accounts. 

HOW TO PROTECT YOURSELF
The biggest opportunities are not tiny spending cuts but larger financial decisions: move idle cash into higher-yield savings, aggressively reduce high-interest credit-card debt, limit unnecessary financing, avoid tapping retirement accounts unless absolutely necessary, and reduce major recurring expenses wherever possible.

BUILD A BIGGER MARGIN FOR ERROR
The economy is not necessarily collapsing, but financial pressure is concentrated among households with the least flexibility. Building several months of liquid savings, eliminating expensive debt, keeping fixed costs low, and preventing lifestyle inflation from consuming every raise can create significantly more financial breathing room if conditions worsen.

snippet.description:
Download Rocket Money and get a trial of Premium+ today at: https://RocketMoney.com/Graham | Let's discuss the bond market collapse, rising interest rates, and how this is going to affect the housing market - Enjoy! Add me on Instagram: GPStephan

START BUILDING WEALTH WITH MY FREE NEWSLETTER: https://grahamstephan.substack.com

BOND MARKET COLLAPSE
Mortgage rates have surged to roughly 7.5% while long-term Treasury yields are near their highest levels in more than 20 years. Because bond prices and yields move in opposite directions, rising yields mean investors are demanding significantly higher returns to lend money to the government. That matters because Treasury yields effectively set the baseline for mortgages, corporate debt, stocks, real estate, and almost every other asset.

INFLATION AND OIL ARE PUSHING RATES HIGHER
Inflation remains elevated while oil has moved back above $100 per barrel. At the same time, negotiations surrounding the Strait of Hormuz have broken down, creating the possibility of even higher energy prices. If oil stays elevated, inflation could remain stubborn, forcing the Federal Reserve to keep rates higher or potentially raise them further.

THE GOVERNMENT DEBT PROBLEM
The United States is running roughly $2 trillion annual deficits while constantly issuing new Treasury bonds to finance spending. The problem is that this new supply is hitting the market at the same time investors are demanding higher yields. Higher borrowing costs then increase government interest expense, which contributes to larger deficits and even more borrowing.

HOUSING DEMAND IS BREAKING DOWN
Higher mortgage rates are hitting transactions before prices. Mortgage applications have fallen toward levels not seen since the early 1990s, while Redfin reports 58% more sellers than buyers. In markets including Las Vegas, Miami, Houston, Orlando, and Nashville, there are more than two sellers for every buyer. Builders and sellers are increasingly using price cuts and concessions to move inventory.

HOME PRICES COULD FACE MORE PRESSURE
National home prices are still slightly higher than a year ago, but after adjusting for inflation, real prices are already declining. If mortgage rates stay above 7%, affordability becomes increasingly difficult. At current rates, the median home would need to fall roughly 14%, or about $62,000, to produce the same monthly payment buyers could have received earlier in the year.

THE DEBT SPIRAL
US national debt has crossed $40 trillion, and interest expense has already exceeded $1 trillion this fiscal year. Much of the debt was originally issued at lower rates, meaning refinancing it at today's yields gradually increases the government's interest burden. Every additional percentage point of borrowing cost on debt held by the public eventually represents hundreds of billions of dollars in additional annual interest.

BONDS ARE NOW COMPETING WITH STOCKS
Long-duration Treasury bonds have suffered enormous price declines, with TLT more than 50% below its 2020 peak. Meanwhile, yields have risen enough that Treasuries can now offer returns comparable to the S&P 500's earnings yield. That gives investors less incentive to accept stock-market risk unless expected returns are substantially higher.

BONDS ARE ALSO COMPETING WITH RENTAL PROPERTY
Treasury yields have climbed to roughly the same level as rental-property rates. An investor can potentially earn similar income from government bonds without tenants, repairs, property management, or many of the risks involved with owning real estate. If rates remain this high, rental-property prices may eventually need to fall for expected returns to become competitive again.

WHAT HAPPENS NEXT
If oil falls, inflation cools, and the Fed avoids additional tightening, yields and mortgage rates could decline. If oil remains above $100, inflation stays elevated, and mortgage rates approach 8%, housing demand would face more pressure. Unlike 2008, however, most homeowners have significant equity and low fixed-rate mortgages, making a slow inflation-adjusted decline or prolonged stagnation more plausible than widespread forced selling. Markets with heavy construction, excess inventory, and investor ownership would likely feel the pressure first.

snippet.title: “$0 Tax On ALL Profits!” - This NEW Housing Market Proposal Is INSANE
snippet.description:
Go to https://surfshark.com/graham or use code GRAHAM at checkout to get 4 extra months of Surfshark VPN! | Let's talk about a potentially new new housing market proposal to remove capital gains tax, and the impact this would have across the entire housing market - Enjoy! Add me on Instagram: GPStephan

Join The Mastermind: http://www.entertheindex.com/

START BUILDING WEALTH WITH MY FREE NEWSLETTER: https://grahamstephan.substack.com

$0 TAX ON HOME SALE PROFITS?
There are discussions around dramatically expanding the capital gains exclusion when Americans sell real estate, including the possibility of allowing homeowners to exclude as much as $1 million in profit. If something like this became law, it could have major consequences for homeowners, investors, buyers, sellers, and the entire housing market.

THE CURRENT CAPITAL GAINS EXCLUSION
Right now, homeowners can generally exclude up to $250,000 of capital gains when filing single, or $500,000 when married filing jointly, as long as they owned and lived in the property for at least two of the previous five years. Those limits were established in 1997 and have never been indexed to inflation, even as home prices have increased substantially.

WHY THE $500,000 LIMIT MATTERS
For longtime homeowners in expensive markets, the existing exclusion can leave a significant amount of appreciation subject to federal capital gains taxes. Simply adjusting the original $500,000 married exclusion for inflation would put it at roughly $1 million today.

COULD INVESTMENT PROPERTIES QUALIFY?
This is where the potential impact becomes much larger. Rental properties generally do not qualify for the primary residence exclusion unless the owner satisfies the residency requirements. If lawmakers ever extended a large capital gains exclusion to investment properties, millions of landlords could suddenly have a major financial incentive to sell.

MILLIONS OF RENTALS COULD HIT THE MARKET
There are roughly 49 million rental units throughout the United States. If even a small percentage of investors decided to sell because of a temporary tax incentive, the resulting increase in inventory could be substantial, especially in investor heavy markets such as Las Vegas, Phoenix, Tampa, Atlanta, and Dallas.

WHAT THIS COULD DO TO HOME PRICES
More inventory means more competition among sellers. In markets where supply begins exceeding buyer demand, sellers may have to lower prices to attract buyers. If landlords are also receiving a large tax benefit from selling, they could be more willing to accept lower offers while still walking away with more money after taxes.

WHO WOULD BENEFIT MOST?
The biggest immediate beneficiaries would likely be longtime homeowners with substantial appreciation, particularly in expensive housing markets. Buyers could benefit from increased inventory and potentially lower prices. However, homeowners without large gains could face more competition, while some renters could be displaced if landlords decide to sell.

THIS IDEA ALREADY EXISTS IN CONGRESS
The bipartisan More Homes on the Market Act would double the current primary residence exclusion to $500,000 for individuals and $1 million for married couples while indexing the limits to inflation going forward. Other proposals have suggested eliminating the caps entirely.

COULD THIS ACTUALLY PASS?
Tax legislation can potentially move through budget reconciliation with a simple Senate majority, but there are major restrictions involving deficits and long term costs. That makes any major new tax break complicated and potentially temporary.

INVESTMENT PROPERTIES ARE STILL SPECULATIVE
As of now, there is no existing bill in Congress that would give every investment property a $1 million capital gains exclusion. Most concrete proposals currently focus on increasing the exclusion for primary residences.

WOULD THIS FIX HOUSING?
Expanding the exclusion could encourage more owners to sell and temporarily increase housing supply, but it would not solve the underlying shortage of homes. The larger long term issue remains housing construction, development costs, zoning, labor, and the ability to build enough homes to keep pace with demand.

snippet.description:

START BUILDING WEALTH WITH MY FREE NEWSLETTER: https://grahamstephan.substack.com

THE FED JUST RAISED INTEREST RATES
For the first time since 2023, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates by 25 basis points, potentially marking the end of the rate-cutting cycle. Inflation remains above target, the labor market is still relatively strong, and policymakers appear to believe the economy can withstand higher borrowing costs.

WHY INFLATION IS STILL A PROBLEM
Producer prices and consumer inflation have remained elevated, while higher energy prices continue adding pressure throughout the economy. As long as inflation stays stubborn, the Federal Reserve has less room to lower rates—and potentially more justification to keep them higher for longer.

THE BOND MARKET IS ALREADY RAISING RATES
The Federal Reserve directly controls short-term rates, but longer-term borrowing costs are determined largely by the bond market. Treasury yields have already moved substantially higher as investors demand greater compensation for inflation, government borrowing, and long-term uncertainty.

WHAT HIGHER RATES MEAN FOR STOCKS
Stocks have spent much of the last few years benefiting from expectations of cheaper money. Strong economic data can now work against the market if it gives the Federal Reserve more room to maintain higher rates. At the same time, elevated bond yields increasingly compete with stocks for investor capital.

THE HOUSING MARKET IS FEELING IT
Mortgage rates have moved higher while housing inventory has increased, giving buyers more options in certain markets. Some cities are already experiencing year-over-year price declines, although historically higher rates alone have not necessarily caused home prices to fall.

WHY LOWER RATES DON’T ALWAYS HELP HOUSING
Interest rates typically fall when economic conditions are weakening. That means lower mortgage rates can arrive alongside slower job growth, falling inflation, or recession concerns—which may offset the benefit of cheaper financing.

ANOTHER RATE HIKE COULD STILL HAPPEN
The Federal Reserve’s economic projections suggest that rates could remain elevated, with the possibility of another increase before the end of the year depending on inflation and economic data.

WHAT HAPPENS NEXT
The economy appears to be heading toward one of two very different outcomes: persistent inflation, higher debt, elevated interest rates and continued market volatility—or a major productivity boom driven by artificial intelligence that allows economic growth to catch up with today’s valuations.

WHAT I’M DOING
Rather than trying to perfectly predict every Federal Reserve decision, I’m sticking with a long-term strategy: consistently investing, dollar-cost averaging through volatility, and paying close attention to inflation, oil prices, Treasury yields, employment and economic growth.

snippet.title: I Paid Off My 2.875% Mortgage…Dave Ramsey Was Right
snippet.description:
Get free life insurance quotes from America's top insurers and start saving today with Policygenius: https://policygenius.com/graham Thanks to Policygenius for sponsoring this video! | Let's talk about paying off your mortgage and the benefits of being debt free | Add me on Instagram: GPStephan

START BUILDING WEALTH WITH MY FREE NEWSLETTER: https://grahamstephan.substack.com

KEEPING LOW-INTEREST DEBT
For years, I argued that paying off a sub-3% mortgage was mathematically irrational. But after asking nearly 4 million people on Twitter whether they regretted paying off cheap debt, almost no one said yes.

HOW DEBT BECAME A TOOL
Growing up, I was taught that all debt was bad. I avoided credit cards, car payments, and loans entirely. That philosophy changed at 21 when I tried to finance real estate and was denied because I had no credit history. I realized debt wasn’t inherently bad; it was a financial tool. If I could borrow at 5% and invest at 12%, the 7% spread represented profit on money I never originally had. That realization became the foundation of my real estate strategy.

HOW LEVERAGE BUILT MY WEALTH
Over the following decade, I used excellent credit and cheap fixed-rate mortgages to buy real estate instead of paying cash. Properties could generate rental returns above the mortgage rate while appreciation multiplied returns on my original down payment. With mortgages around 3–3.6%, inflation also reduced the real cost of the debt over time. This strategy helped create millions of dollars in equity, which is why I spent years telling people not to pay off cheap mortgages early.

THE MENTAL COST OF DEBT
What I failed to account for was the psychological burden attached to every loan. Even an affordable mortgage creates an ongoing obligation: payments continue if income falls, tenants leave, markets crash, or you want to stop working. When millions of dollars of debt disappeared from my accounts, I realized those obligations had occupied mental space even though I was never worried about making the payments. 

WHY DEBT FREEDOM FEELS DIFFERENT
Research suggests that eliminating debt can reduce anxiety and improve decision-making and cognitive performance. Interestingly, the number of debts eliminated may matter more psychologically than the dollar amount eliminated. Closing several separate obligations can therefore provide a larger mental benefit than simply reducing one large balance. That helps explain why debt freedom can feel disproportionately valuable even when it isn’t mathematically optimal.

PAYING OFF A 3% MORTGAGE IS EMOTIONAL, NOT FINANCIAL
Paying the mortgage off means voluntarily giving up expected returns. But the calculation ignores peace of mind. Financial well-being and how secure people feel about their money can materially affect happiness, meaning the value of simplicity and lower stress deserves to be included even if it cannot easily be modeled in a spreadsheet.

DON’T SACRIFICE YOUR LIQUIDITY
Debt freedom can also be taken too far. Using every available dollar to pay off a mortgage converts highly liquid cash into illiquid home equity. If an emergency happens, you cannot simply ask the mortgage company to return your money. Research also found that some households accelerated mortgage payments while neglecting more valuable tax-advantaged retirement opportunities, leaving themselves financially worse off.

THE PRACTICAL ORDER OF OPERATIONS
The priority should still be an emergency fund first. After that, take advantage of an employer 401(k) match and aggressively eliminate high-interest debt, roughly anything above 7–8%. Only after those priorities are handled should paying off extremely cheap debt become a serious consideration. At that point, the decision depends less on maximizing every percentage point and more on how much you personally value simplicity, flexibility, and peace of mind.

SIMPLICITY HAS VALUE
As I’ve gotten older, squeezing every possible dollar out of leverage matters less to me than having fewer obligations, fewer accounts, and fewer things to think about. The purpose of building wealth eventually becomes having more freedom—not simply maximizing the spreadsheet forever.

The priority should still be an emergency fund first. After that, take advantage of an employer 401(k) match and aggressively eliminate high-interest debt, roughly anything above 7–8%. Only after those priorities are handled should paying off extremely cheap debt become a serious consideration. At that point, the decision depends less on maximizing every percentage point and more on how much you personally value simplicity, flexibility, and peace of mind.

SIMPLICITY HAS VALUE
As I’ve gotten older, squeezing every possible dollar out of leverage matters less to me than having fewer obligations, fewer accounts, and fewer things to think about. The purpose of building wealth eventually becomes having more freedom—not simply maximizing the spreadsheet forever.

AMERICA’S DEBT PROBLEM IS GETTING STRANGER
Starting September 9th, the Treasury is set to double the amount of debt it buys back, which the script frames as the government effectively borrowing new money to help manage existing debt. The concern is that the U.S. is increasingly relying on more borrowing to deal with an already enormous debt load, raising the question of what happens when the solution to excessive debt becomes even more debt.

WHY TREASURY BUYBACKS MATTER
The government normally finances itself by issuing Treasury bonds, then issuing new debt when older debt matures. The problem is that inflation and higher rates mean investors are demanding greater returns to lend the government money. Treasury buybacks are intended to improve liquidity and absorb some unwanted older securities rather than allowing yields to rise uncontrollably. Critics argue this treats the symptoms rather than the underlying problem of rising debt, inflation, and weaker demand for government bonds.

KEVIN WARSH’S 5-PART FED PLAN
The script says new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh laid out five major themes at Jackson Hole. First, the Fed intends to communicate less and stop constantly signaling future moves. Second, it will allow markets to move independently and react afterward rather than guiding them in advance. Third, inflation must decisively return toward the Fed’s 2% target. Fourth, the economy remains strong enough to tolerate tighter policy, with unemployment around 4.1% and financial conditions not viewed as especially restrictive. Fifth, Warsh sees AI as a potentially historic productivity breakthrough that could fundamentally reshape economic growth.

SEPTEMBER COULD BRING MORE STOCK MARKET VOLATILITY
Despite higher rates, stocks and housing have remained relatively resilient. However, historically September has been one of the weakest months for stocks, with the script citing data showing positive returns only about 45% of the time and an average decline of roughly 0.6%. Possible explanations include tax-loss harvesting, investors raising cash and lower late-summer trading volumes. At the same time, weakness in September does not automatically mean a larger bear market, and historically the periods following midterm elections have often been considerably stronger.

THE NEXT BIG RISK IS INTEREST RATES
Markets are pricing in the possibility of another Fed rate hike while Treasury yields are already rising substantially on their own. The script argues that market-driven increases could potentially do some of the Fed’s tightening for it, reducing the need for an actual hike. The major level to watch is the 10-year Treasury yield approaching 5%, which is portrayed as an important psychological threshold that could begin creating larger problems throughout stocks, housing, borrowing costs and the broader economy.

A PULLBACK WOULDN’T NECESSARILY MEAN A CRASH
Even very strong stock-market years regularly experience significant declines along the way. Historical midterm-cycle data cited in the script is especially encouraging over longer periods, including the claim that the S&P 500 was higher one year after August 31 in 18 of the previous 19 midterm years. Because of that, a short-term 5–10% correction would not necessarily change the long-term outlook and could simply represent normal volatility.

HOW I’M PREPARING
Rather than making a major portfolio change, the strategy is to remain diversified and avoid reacting emotionally to short-term volatility. The portfolio described is roughly 55% stocks, 20% tax-free municipal bonds, 10% cryptocurrency through a Bitcoin ETF, with the remainder in real estate and other investments. If stocks fall substantially, additional cash could be invested, but there is no urgency to sell existing positions or aggressively buy while uncertainty remains elevated.

snippet.description:
Thanks to SoFi for sponsoring the video! Click here to sign-up for SoFi Crypto: https://sofi.com/graham | Let's discuss the bond market bailout and whether or not we're in a stock market bubble - Enjoy! Add me on Instagram: GPStephan

START BUILDING WEALTH WITH MY FREE NEWSLETTER: https://grahamstephan.substack.com

THE U.S. BAILOUT
The Treasury is preparing for potentially enormous financial intervention as long-term interest rates surge toward levels not seen in nearly 20 years. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has discussed deploying up to $1 trillion, while Treasury has already expanded buybacks of longer-term government debt. 

WHY TREASURY YIELDS ARE SURGING
Investors are increasingly worried that inflation will remain elevated, so they are demanding higher returns to lend money long term. Higher Treasury yields then ripple throughout the economy, increasing mortgage rates, corporate borrowing costs, and government interest expenses.

THE STOCK MARKET IS EXTREMELY EXPENSIVE
Stocks have continued hitting records, but several valuation metrics are flashing warnings. The CAPE ratio is near levels associated with the Dotcom Bubble, the Buffett Indicator has reached record highs, and a relatively small group of AI companies has driven an outsized portion of recent gains. Critics argue this leaves the market vulnerable if expectations around AI begin to disappoint.

THE FIVE BIGGEST AI BUBBLE CONCERNS
Beyond valuations, AI companies are spending enormous amounts on infrastructure before proving they can generate sufficient profits from that investment. Critics also point to circular financing between technology companies, similarities to previous infrastructure bubbles, and extreme concentration of venture capital in AI. Even Sam Altman has acknowledged that investors may be overexcited about the technology.

WHY THIS MIGHT NOT BE A BUBBLE
The bull case is that today's largest technology companies are fundamentally different from Dotcom-era businesses. Nvidia, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, and Amazon generate enormous profits and can finance AI investments largely through existing cash flow. Earnings continue beating expectations, smaller companies are participating in the rally, and the equal-weighted S&P 500 has also reached records, suggesting market strength extends beyond a handful of technology giants.

AI GROWTH IS ALREADY SHOWING UP
AI-related businesses are reporting rapid growth in revenue and usage, potentially supporting today's enormous investments. Valuations are high, but many companies are substantially more profitable than speculative technology businesses were during 2000. Most importantly, expensive markets rarely collapse simply because valuations are high. Usually, they need a catalyst that triggers widespread selling.

WHAT THE DATA SAYS ABOUT FUTURE RETURNS
Stocks are historically expensive, but comparing valuations with the last 30 years makes today's market appear less extreme. Even historically terrible entry points have eventually rewarded investors who remained invested and collected dividends rather than attempting to perfectly time the market.

BUYING AT ALL-TIME HIGHS ISN'T NECESSARILY BAD
Markets naturally spend significant amounts of time near record highs as businesses grow and inflation increases nominal prices. Historically, buying at all-time highs has not dramatically changed long-term returns for patient investors. High valuations can increase downside risk, but they do not reliably predict when a correction will happen.

THE INVESTMENT TAKEAWAY
Markets could continue melting higher as government intervention lowers yields, or an unexpected catalyst could trigger a major correction. Predicting either outcome consistently is nearly impossible. The practical strategy is diversification, maintaining liquidity, investing consistently, and avoiding panic selling.

snippet.description:
You’ve worked hard to build your financial future - Coveron helps you protect it. The first 100 users get 20% off with code GRAHAMSTEPHAN at https://coveron.com/grahamstephan | Let's talk about the Trump Tax Plan, Indexing Capital Gains To Inflation, & the chance of this passing - Add me on Instagram: GPStephan

START BUILDING WEALTH WITH MY FREE NEWSLETTER: https://grahamstephan.substack.com

TRUMP FLOATS A MAJOR CAPITAL GAINS TAX CHANGE
President Trump is reportedly considering changes to capital gains taxes ahead of the midterms, including indexing gains to inflation and dramatically increasing the tax exemption for primary residences. If enacted, the changes could reduce taxes for investors and homeowners while potentially encouraging people sitting on large gains to finally sell.

HOW CAPITAL GAINS TAXES WORK
Investments held for less than one year are generally taxed as ordinary income, with federal rates reaching 37%. Investments held longer than a year receive preferential rates of 0%, 15%, or 20%. Higher-income investors can also owe the 3.8% Net Investment Tax.

INDEXING CAPITAL GAINS TO INFLATION
Currently, the tax code generally taxes nominal profits without adjusting the original investment for inflation. Someone who invested $100,000 decades ago could owe taxes even if their investment merely maintained its purchasing power. The proposed solution would increase an investor's cost basis by inflation. 

A MUCH LARGER HOME SALE EXEMPTION
Homeowners can currently exclude $250K of gains if single or $500K if married when selling a qualifying primary residence. This was established in 1997 and has never been adjusted for inflation, despite enormous increases in home prices.

One proposal could effectively raise the married exemption toward $2 million. A couple with a $1 million gain that might currently owe significant federal tax could potentially owe nothing under a substantially larger exemption.

THE "LOCK-IN EFFECT"
Capital gains taxes can discourage investors and homeowners from selling appreciated assets. Older homeowners in particular may choose to remain in valuable homes rather than trigger a large tax bill. Some instead hold their properties until death, when heirs may receive a stepped-up cost basis.

Increasing the home exemption could encourage those owners to downsize sooner, potentially unlocking additional housing inventory. Lower investment taxes could similarly encourage investors sitting on enormous unrealized gains to rebalance or sell.

WHO BENEFITS THE MOST
The biggest criticism is that capital gains tax reductions disproportionately benefit wealthier households because they own the majority of appreciating financial assets. Lower taxes could increase selling and market liquidity, but they could also worsen the federal deficit while providing relatively little direct benefit to Americans who do not own investments.

THE BIG ROADBLOCK
Despite the headlines, there is currently no formal Trump proposal. The discussion stems from comments by economic advisers indicating Trump is interested in ideas including inflation indexing and a larger home exemption.

Passing major changes through Congress before the midterms appears difficult. Attempting to index gains through Treasury regulations without Congress could also face major legal challenges. Retroactively applying inflation adjustments could potentially cost the government enormous amounts of revenue.

WHAT COULD REALISTICALLY CHANGE
Full inflation indexing appears unlikely, but smaller reforms may have a better chance. Potential changes include increasing and indexing the primary residence exemption, raising the $3,000 annual capital-loss deduction that has remained unchanged since 1977, indexing the Net Investment Income Tax thresholds to inflation, and changing how dividends are taxed.

THE BOTTOM LINE
Eliminating or dramatically reducing capital gains taxes would have enormous implications for investors, housing, government revenue, and asset prices, but the current discussion is far from becoming law. The more realistic outcome would be targeted reforms to tax provisions that have remained frozen for decades, particularly the home-sale exemption and capital-loss deduction.

snippet.description:
Thanks to SoFi for sponsoring the video! Click here to sign-up for SoFi Crypto: https://sofi.com/graham | Let's talk about rising interest rates and what this means for the stock market / housing values - Enjoy! Add me on Instagram: GPStephan

START BUILDING WEALTH WITH MY FREE NEWSLETTER: https://grahamstephan.substack.com

THE MARKET IS PRICING IN A RATE HIKE
For the first time in more than three years, markets are pricing in the possibility of another Federal Reserve rate hike. Inflation is returning, oil has climbed above $100, foreign countries are selling U.S. Treasuries, and long-term borrowing costs are already moving higher. Mortgages, credit cards, and loans could become even more expensive, while people holding cash may benefit from higher yields.

WHY RATES COULD GO HIGHER
The Federal Reserve raises rates to slow inflation by making borrowing more expensive and reducing spending. The problem is that inflation has begun accelerating again as energy prices rise and Treasury yields increase. If inflation remains stubborn while employment and asset prices stay strong, the Fed may decide the economy can withstand additional tightening.

WHAT HIGHER RATES MEAN FOR STOCKS
Higher rates generally pressure stocks because future corporate profits become less valuable and safer investments become more attractive. If government bonds pay more than 4%, investors have less incentive to take substantial risk for slightly higher stock market returns.

However, history suggests rate hikes alone do not necessarily cause crashes. Since the 1960s, stocks have continued trending higher through many tightening cycles. Historically, stocks rose 76% of the time during the six months following a rate hike and 81% of the time over the following year. Economic weakness and recessions tend to matter more than the rate hikes themselves.

HOUSING GETS EVEN MORE EXPENSIVE
Mortgage rates have nearly tripled from their pandemic lows. A $300,000 mortgage that cost roughly $1,265 per month at 3% would cost about $1,900 at 6.5%. Higher rates price buyers out while simultaneously discouraging existing homeowners with cheap mortgages from selling.

Surprisingly, rising mortgage rates have historically not translated directly into falling home prices. Instead, they tend to slow appreciation and reduce transaction volume. Inflation, economic growth, housing supply, and employment often have a greater influence on prices.

THE BOND MARKET IS ALREADY RAISING RATES
Markets are pricing a meaningful probability of a September rate hike, but the bigger story is that long-term rates are already increasing without the Fed doing anything.

The Fed directly controls short-term rates, while mortgages, business borrowing, and other long-term rates are heavily influenced by Treasury markets. Investors worried about inflation are demanding higher yields, while foreign selling of Treasuries adds additional pressure. In effect, the bond market is tightening financial conditions before the Fed even votes.

WHO LOSES FROM HIGHER RATES
People with variable-rate debt are among the most exposed because their payments can increase immediately. The U.S. government is another major loser, with $38.5 trillion of debt and interest expenses approaching $1 trillion annually. Refinancing old government debt at higher rates could substantially increase future interest costs.

Job seekers could also suffer if higher borrowing costs cause companies to slow expansion and freeze hiring, particularly as the labor market is already cooling.

WHO BENEFITS
Cash becomes increasingly attractive because high-yield savings accounts and short-term government debt can generate meaningful returns with limited risk. Homeowners who locked in mortgages below 4% are also in an unusually strong position because their payments remain fixed while inflation gradually reduces the real value of their debt.

Ultimately, higher rates could create short-term pain while helping bring inflation and excessive asset valuations back under control. The key risk is whether policymakers can slow the economy enough to stabilize prices without triggering a deeper recession.

localized.description:
Thanks to SoFi for sponsoring the video! Click here to sign-up for SoFi Crypto: https://sofi.com/graham | Let's talk about rising interest rates and what this means for the stock market / housing values - Enjoy! Add me on Instagram: GPStephan

START BUILDING WEALTH WITH MY FREE NEWSLETTER: https://grahamstephan.substack.com

THE MARKET IS PRICING IN A RATE HIKE
For the first time in more than three years, markets are pricing in the possibility of another Federal Reserve rate hike. Inflation is returning, oil has climbed above $100, foreign countries are selling U.S. Treasuries, and long-term borrowing costs are already moving higher. Mortgages, credit cards, and loans could become even more expensive, while people holding cash may benefit from higher yields.

WHY RATES COULD GO HIGHER
The Federal Reserve raises rates to slow inflation by making borrowing more expensive and reducing spending. The problem is that inflation has begun accelerating again as energy prices rise and Treasury yields increase. If inflation remains stubborn while employment and asset prices stay strong, the Fed may decide the economy can withstand additional tightening.

WHAT HIGHER RATES MEAN FOR STOCKS
Higher rates generally pressure stocks because future corporate profits become less valuable and safer investments become more attractive. If government bonds pay more than 4%, investors have less incentive to take substantial risk for slightly higher stock market returns.

However, history suggests rate hikes alone do not necessarily cause crashes. Since the 1960s, stocks have continued trending higher through many tightening cycles. Historically, stocks rose 76% of the time during the six months following a rate hike and 81% of the time over the following year. Economic weakness and recessions tend to matter more than the rate hikes themselves.

HOUSING GETS EVEN MORE EXPENSIVE
Mortgage rates have nearly tripled from their pandemic lows. A $300,000 mortgage that cost roughly $1,265 per month at 3% would cost about $1,900 at 6.5%. Higher rates price buyers out while simultaneously discouraging existing homeowners with cheap mortgages from selling.

Surprisingly, rising mortgage rates have historically not translated directly into falling home prices. Instead, they tend to slow appreciation and reduce transaction volume. Inflation, economic growth, housing supply, and employment often have a greater influence on prices.

THE BOND MARKET IS ALREADY RAISING RATES
Markets are pricing a meaningful probability of a September rate hike, but the bigger story is that long-term rates are already increasing without the Fed doing anything.

The Fed directly controls short-term rates, while mortgages, business borrowing, and other long-term rates are heavily influenced by Treasury markets. Investors worried about inflation are demanding higher yields, while foreign selling of Treasuries adds additional pressure. In effect, the bond market is tightening financial conditions before the Fed even votes.

WHO LOSES FROM HIGHER RATES
People with variable-rate debt are among the most exposed because their payments can increase immediately. The U.S. government is another major loser, with $38.5 trillion of debt and interest expenses approaching $1 trillion annually. Refinancing old government debt at higher rates could substantially increase future interest costs.

Job seekers could also suffer if higher borrowing costs cause companies to slow expansion and freeze hiring, particularly as the labor market is already cooling.

WHO BENEFITS
Cash becomes increasingly attractive because high-yield savings accounts and short-term government debt can generate meaningful returns with limited risk. Homeowners who locked in mortgages below 4% are also in an unusually strong position because their payments remain fixed while inflation gradually reduces the real value of their debt.

Ultimately, higher rates could create short-term pain while helping bring inflation and excessive asset valuations back under control. The key risk is whether policymakers can slow the economy enough to stabilize prices without triggering a deeper recession.

snippet.title: Japan’s Currency Crisis Is Now America’s Problem
snippet.description:
Go to https://surfshark.com/graham or use code GRAHAM at checkout to get 4 extra months of Surfshark VPN! Let's talk about the Japenese Yen, while they're selling US Dollars to support their currency, and why this is causing interest rates to increase - Enjoy! Add me on Instagram: GPStephan

START BUILDING WEALTH WITH MY FREE NEWSLETTER: https://grahamstephan.substack.com

THE YEN CRISIS IS BECOMING AN AMERICAN PROBLEM
U.S. banks have reportedly been warned to prepare for a possible coordinated intervention in the Japanese yen after the currency fell near its weakest level in roughly 40 years. Japan may have already sold nearly $59 billion in U.S. dollar assets to support the yen, raising concerns that continued intervention could disrupt Treasury markets, interest rates, and global asset prices.

HOW THE YEN CARRY TRADE WORKS
Japan maintained extremely low interest rates for decades because of weak demand, low inflation, and an aging economy. Meanwhile, the United States rapidly increased rates to fight inflation. That created a profitable trade where investors could borrow cheaply in yen, convert the money into dollars, and buy higher-yielding U.S. Treasuries.

Investors could earn the difference between Japanese and American interest rates, while also benefiting if the yen continued weakening. This helped send capital into the United States and supported demand for dollars, Treasuries, stocks, and other financial assets.

WHY THE TRADE IS UNWINDING
The strategy works until Japan intervenes to strengthen its currency. Japan recently sold dollars and bought yen in an emergency attempt to stop the currency from collapsing. When the yen suddenly rises, investors who borrowed in yen may rush to close their positions, selling U.S. assets and converting the proceeds back into Japanese currency.

Because Japan is the largest foreign holder of U.S. Treasuries, those sales could add substantial supply to the market. Treasury prices would fall and yields would rise, potentially increasing mortgage rates, consumer borrowing costs, corporate financing expenses, and pressure on stock valuations.

WHY LONG-TERM INTEREST RATES ARE RISING
The Federal Reserve directly controls short-term policy rates, but longer-term rates are determined by supply and demand. When foreign governments and investors buy Treasuries, yields generally decline. When they sell, buyers demand a higher return to absorb the additional supply.

Japan is not the only potential seller. Foreign demand for U.S. debt has weakened as other countries face inflation, rising expenses, and greater funding needs. That means the Treasury market could remain under pressure even if the immediate yen crisis stabilizes.

WHY THE UNITED STATES MAY INTERVENE
The United States could potentially buy yen with dollars to reduce the pressure on Japan to liquidate American assets. The goal would not simply be to rescue Japan. It would also be to protect the value of U.S. Treasuries and prevent a disorderly fire sale from pushing American interest rates sharply higher.

WHY INTERVENTION MAY NOT WORK FOR LONG
Japan attempted a similar intervention in 2024, spending heavily to support the yen. The currency initially rebounded but resumed falling within weeks. The latest intervention also produced only a brief recovery before traders pushed the yen weaker again.

The underlying problem is the gap between Japanese and American interest rates. As long as investors can borrow cheaply in Japan and earn significantly more in the United States, the incentive behind the carry trade remains. Currency intervention addresses the immediate decline but does not remove that structural imbalance.

WHAT HAPPENS NEXT
The safest outcome would be a gradual adjustment where Japan slowly raises rates while the Federal Reserve eventually lowers them. That would reduce the interest-rate gap without forcing investors to unwind positions all at once. The dangerous outcome would be if the yen strengthens suddenly, leveraged investors could be forced to sell assets, producing sharp volatility across bonds, stocks, and currencies.

THE INVESTMENT TAKEAWAY
The most likely outcome is short-term volatility followed by a gradual normalization as Japan tightens policy and the carry trade becomes less attractive.

snippet.title: The AI Bubble Just Collapsed — A Warning For America
snippet.description:
Take your personal data back with Incogni! Use code GRAHAM at the link below and get 60% off an annual plan: https://incogni.com/graham | Let's discuss the South Korea Stock Market AI Bubble, Why Prices Are Falling, and Similarities In The United States - Enjoy! Add me on Instagram: GPStephan

START BUILDING WEALTH WITH MY FREE NEWSLETTER: https://grahamstephan.substack.com

SOUTH KOREA'S MARKET CRASH: COULD THE U.S. BE NEXT?
South Korea's stock market recently suffered its fastest and largest decline on record after falling more than 20% in just a few weeks. The concern is that many of the same ingredients behind that crash now exist in the United States, including heavy AI concentration, record valuations, rising leverage, and widespread investor optimism.

WHAT CAUSED KOREA'S COLLAPSE
The KOSPI had become heavily concentrated in just two semiconductor companies, Samsung and SK Hynix, which accounted for more than half the index. After regulators approved leveraged single-stock ETFs, retail investors poured billions into products that magnified gains and losses. When regulators later warned the market had become overheated, selling accelerated. Falling stock prices forced leveraged funds to sell even more shares, creating a self-reinforcing downward spiral that quickly erased months of gains.

WHY INVESTORS ARE COMPARING THE U.S.
The U.S. market shares several characteristics with Korea. The largest ten companies now account for roughly 37% of the S&P 500, technology dominates the index, valuations rank among the highest in history, and margin debt has climbed to record levels. Professional investors also hold unusually low cash balances, while corporate insiders are selling shares at an elevated pace. Although none of these factors guarantees a decline, they suggest the market is increasingly dependent on a relatively small group of companies continuing to perform exceptionally well.

THE BULL CASE
Wall Street remains broadly optimistic. Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Citi, and several other major firms still expect the S&P 500 to finish the year higher, driven primarily by strong corporate earnings and AI-related investment. Earnings growth has remained robust, most companies continue beating expectations, market leadership has broadened beyond the largest technology stocks, corporate buybacks remain strong, and credit markets show few signs of financial stress. Unlike the dot-com era, today's largest technology companies generate enormous profits while funding AI expansion largely from existing cash flow rather than speculative financing.

THE BEAR CASE
The risks remain substantial. Current valuations assume near-perfect execution, continued AI monetization, strong earnings growth, stable interest rates, and no recession. If earnings disappoint even modestly or valuation multiples simply return toward historical norms, stocks could experience significant declines without a financial crisis. Rising oil prices, elevated leverage, record margin debt, and limited cash available to buy future dips could amplify any correction through forced selling. Several strategists continue forecasting meaningful downside under less favorable economic scenarios.

IS AMERICA LIKE KOREA?
There are important differences. The U.S. market is far more diversified, supported by institutional investors, pension funds, global capital, and automatic retirement contributions. While concentration is elevated, it is nowhere near Korea's dependence on just two companies, and leveraged single-stock products remain a much smaller portion of the overall market. Those structural differences make a Korea-style collapse less likely, even if the market experiences a significant correction.

THE MAIN TAKEAWAY
The lesson is not that America will repeat Korea's crash. It is that concentration, leverage, and investor euphoria can quickly turn a healthy rally into a painful selloff. Rather than trying to predict the next correction, the more durable strategy is maintaining an emergency fund, avoiding leverage, diversifying across multiple asset classes, and staying invested for the long term. Even if markets become volatile, history suggests disciplined investors who avoid panic and continue investing have consistently produced the best long-term results.
